past.date: Tue 4 Aug 2026, after the US close (Wed 5 Aug, about 4am Singapore)
past.vs: Revenue $11.54bn, +50% vs a year earlier, vs about $11.30bn consensus (+2.1%). Adjusted EPS $1.66 vs $1.61 expected (+3.2%).
past.guide: September quarter: revenue about $13.0bn ± $0.3bn (+41% vs a year earlier) vs about $12.54bn consensus; adjusted gross margin about 56%, flat.
past.reaction: Shares −7.1% the next day while the S&P 500 fell 0.2%. A few analysts had been hoping for guidance closer to $14bn (Briefs).
take: Data Center doubled. $6.72bn, +107% vs a year earlier; 58% of revenue in the quarter (54% over the last 4 quarters).
PCs strong, gaming weak. Client $3.06bn (+23%); Gaming $0.78bn (−31%); Embedded $0.98bn (+19%), all vs a year earlier.

Margin stalled at a high level. Adjusted gross margin 56%, up 13 points vs a year earlier, but that year-ago quarter carried a one-off $800m write-down of MI308 chips blocked for China. It is guided flat at about 56% for September; investors wanted further improvement.
Helios in full production. Shipments from the end of the Sep quarter, so most rack revenue lands in Q4 2026 and 2027.

New AI customers. Anthropic agreed to deploy up to 2 GW of MI450 chips (GW = gigawatts of data-centre power the chips draw; first 1 GW from H1 2027), and AMD will invest up to $5bn in Anthropic's shares. Management expects Data Center to more than double in 2027.
Opaque mix. AMD does not split AI chips from server CPUs, so the AI share of growth is not visible.
past.impact: Demand indicators strong (DM3, DM4a, DM4b bullish), but the shares fell: the stock is priced for more than a normal beat.

lead: AMD reads Buy at +50 on a −100 to +100 scale, up from +48 yesterday (Buy line +30): demand and the price trend score the maximum, but investors already pay a steep premium, and the reading depends on AI spending and the price momentum both holding up.
bullets: Demand is at full strength, but it is one bet. Demand scores +100: revenue grew 50.1% vs a year earlier, faster than its 34.8% average of the prior four quarters; Data Center grew 107% and PC chips 22.5% (Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier), and the big-4 cloud firms' capital spending 77%. Guidance (40.6% growth) beat the roughly 35.6% expected, and the 2027 earnings forecast rose 18.2% in 90 days ($15.58 vs $13.18 a share). Almost all of these track AI data-centre spending, so a pause there would turn them together. Gross margin is up 5.6 points (last 4 quarters vs the 4 a year earlier), but about 2.7 points of that comes from a one-off $800m China chip write-down in the year-ago figures.

It is priced for it, before counting dilution. Valuation scores −63: investors pay 47% more per dollar of expected next-12-month profit than the peer median (45.1x vs 30.7x forward P/E). On company value including debt vs last-12-month operating profit before depreciation (EV/EBITDA) it is 103.5x vs 30.0x, a gap overstated because AMD's revenue is growing 50% a year. Only the growth-adjusted P/E is in line (0.6 vs 0.7, 12% below the peer median). Not scored: warrants to OpenAI and Meta could add up to 320m shares (about 20% of today's), which would lift the forward P/E to about 54x if all vested.

The money backdrop is mixed. Liquidity scores +40: volume on up days is 2.62x that on down days (last 20 trading days) and institutions already holding AMD added a net 3.80% of shares last quarter (new and closed positions not counted), but the dollar index is 1.80 points higher than 20 trading days ago and markets now give a 34% chance of a Fed rate rise on 28 Oct, up from 27% a month earlier.

The trend is strongly up, and stretched. Price scores +100: AMD is 65.1% above its 200-day average and 14.7 points ahead of its peers over the last 3 months; it closed at $611.76, +0.7% on the day vs −0.25% for the S&P 500. That distance trips the stretch flag: a sign the run may be overextended and prone to sharp pullbacks (timing context only, not scored). The Buy leans on momentum: with a neutral price trend the composite would be about +25, which is Hold.
Not yet a confirmed call. Day 2 of the 10 trading days of score history needed. Next big test: results, expected 3 Nov (date not yet announced).
defects: Staging build, second day of history: the call needs 10 trading days of scores before it can be confirmed.
VL3 (P/E vs own history) is removed for AMD and left out of the score (applied by the shared engine from 30 Sep): trailing P/E is distorted by 2023 losses and Xilinx amortisation.

EV/EBITDA uses last-12-month EBITDA (free source); for a company growing 50% a year this makes AMD look expensive. Debt in EV ($4.3bn) includes leases (Yahoo); AMD reports $3.2bn of borrowings, a 0.1% effect on EV.
Forward P/E uses 2027 earnings forecasts (AMD's next fiscal year), not strictly the next 12 months; peers use their own next fiscal years, which end at different dates.

Gross margin trend (DM6) uses reported margins: the year-ago 4 quarters include a one-off $800m MI308 write-down, which adds about 2.7 of the 5.6-point rise. DM6 would still score bullish without it (about +2.9 points).
OpenAI and Meta warrants (up to 320m shares, about 20% of today's shares) are not reflected in P/E or any score; see shareholder notes.
Chain C1 has no watch number yet: TSMC's share price (TSM) is requested from the Framework chat.
Chain C2 watches Micron's share price as a stand-in for memory prices.
Guidance, Data Center, Client and cloud capex inputs (DM3, DM4a, DM4b, DM5) are entered from results releases, so they update quarterly. The DM3 consensus is from a secondary source (approximate).
Institutional change (LQ3) counts changes in existing positions only.

DC.sells: EPYC server processors, Instinct AI chips (MI350, MI450, Helios racks), Pensando networking chips and data-center FPGAs.
DC.buyers: Cloud giants and AI labs (Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, OpenAI, Anthropic), governments and large companies.
pos: Highest growth: +107% in the Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier (+55% over the last 4 quarters); now most of AMD's revenue.
Margin rising: 29% segment operating margin over the last 4 quarters vs 21% a year earlier (31% in the latest quarter).
Multi-year supply deals (OpenAI up to 6 GW, Meta up to 6 GW, Anthropic up to 2 GW) give more visibility than one-off orders.
Server processors are sticky: customers standardise on a platform for years.
neg: Not recurring: hardware sold per order, no subscription income.
Concentrated: a handful of very large buyers decide most orders, and they negotiate hard on price.

Some demand is supported by AMD's own shares and money: OpenAI and Meta get up to 160m AMD shares each as they take delivery, and AMD is investing up to $5bn in Anthropic alongside its 2 GW commitment.
Tied to the AI spending cycle (chain C1); a pause in AI budgets hits here first.
Export rules can wipe out profit quickly: an $800m China charge turned the segment to a loss in Q2 2025.
Full racks (Helios) include more bought-in parts such as memory, which may lower the margin percentage (a risk, not yet seen).

CL.sells: Ryzen processors for desktop and laptop PCs, including AI PC chips.
CL.buyers: PC makers (Lenovo, HP, Dell, Asus) and PC builders; ultimately consumers and businesses.
pos: Taking share from Intel: +23% in the Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier while the PC market is squeezed.
Big and familiar brand; helps AMD sell to the same business customers in servers.
neg: Lower margin: 18% segment operating margin (Client and Gaming combined, last 4 quarters), about 11 points below Data Center.
One-off, seasonal consumer sales; nothing recurring.
Price competition from Intel, Qualcomm and now NVIDIA (RTX Spark PC chips from autumn 2026).
Memory price rises make PCs dearer, which can cut demand (chain C2).

GA.sells: Custom chips for Sony PlayStation and Microsoft Xbox consoles, and Radeon graphics cards.
pos: Console chips come from multi-year contracts with Sony and Microsoft: predictable volumes and little extra R&D.
A new console generation would lift revenue again (timing not announced).
neg: Shrinking now: −31% in the Jun 2026 quarter vs a year earlier, as current consoles are late in their life (though +30% over the last 4 quarters vs the 4 before, after the 2025 console ramp).
Thin margins: the gaming part earned 3-18% operating margin in 2022-24, when AMD still reported it separately.
Graphics cards lose share to NVIDIA.

EM.sells: Xilinx FPGAs and adaptive chips, plus embedded Ryzen and EPYC, for factories, cars, telecoms, medical, aerospace and defence.
EM.buyers: Thousands of equipment makers (industrial, auto, communications, defence).
pos: Highest segment margin: 37% over the last 4 quarters.
The closest thing AMD has to recurring revenue: chips are designed into equipment that is built and sold for 10+ years.
Many small customers: no single buyer dominates.
Steady cash generator with low extra investment.
neg: Slow growth: +5% over the last 4 quarters vs +40% for AMD as a whole; the latest quarter (+19% vs a year earlier) is a rebound from a low base.
Margin falling: 37% vs 50% three years earlier (last 4 quarters each).
Swings with customers' stock levels: revenue fell 46% from Q1 2023 to Q1 2024 as customers ran down inventories.
Now only 9% of revenue (last 4 quarters), so it cushions the company less than it did in 2023.

shift.title: What the shift means for AMD
pos: Higher profit per dollar of sales, but not from the mix: segment operating margin rose to 26% (last 4 quarters) from 21% a year earlier because Data Center's own margin rose (29% vs 21%). The shift in mix itself took about 0.4 points off, because high-margin Embedded shrank.
Free cash flow was 18.7% of revenue over the last 4 quarters ($7.7bn) vs 11.8% a year earlier ($3.5bn).
Faster growth: revenue is up 115% in three years (Jun 2026 quarter vs Jun 2023 quarter), almost all from Data Center.
neg: Less diversified: Data Center is 54% of revenue over the last 4 quarters (58% in the Jun 2026 quarter), up from 27% three years earlier. A slowdown in AI budgets would hit AMD harder than before.
Less recurring: the steadiest business (Embedded) fell from 26% to 9% of revenue, and Gaming from 30% to 9% (last 4 quarters vs the 4 quarters to Jun 2023).
More concentrated: a few very large customers now drive most growth, which gives them pricing power; two of them hold warrants for AMD shares.
